title: Impact of extraction methods on the properties of Carica papaya pseudostem fibers from Cameroon used as reinforcement in

predicted_errors.error_location: Introduction, paragraph on Cameroon papaya production
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The paper states that Cameroon has an annual papaya output of "44 tons" while ranking 64th globally. This is almost certainly a factor-of-1,000 error: Cameroon papaya production is reported in tens of thousands of tonnes, not 44 tonnes. A production of only 44 tonnes could not plausibly be described as generating a large national mass of pseudostem agricultural waste.

The text attributes prior diameter results to "Betene et al. [30], Mono et al. [6]." However, in the methods, reference [30] is explicitly identified as ISO 3344: "samples made anhydrous in a ventilated oven in accordance with ISO 3344 [30]." The same reference number cannot simultaneously denote an ISO standard and a paper by Betene et al.; at least one citation is wrong.

The abstract says diameter decreased with increasing NaOH concentration. The reported mean diameters are 196.33 ± 4 μm at 2.5% NaOH, 221.94 ± 6 μm at 5% NaOH, and 219.31 ± 4 μm at 7.5% NaOH. Diameter therefore increases substantially from 2.5% to 5% and is not monotonically decreasing with NaOH concentration. It is lower than the water-retted value (302.02 ± 4 μm), but the claimed concentration trend is false.

The reported dry-fiber yield rises from 19.92% to 28.63% as NaOH rises from 2.5% to 7.5%, but this increase is attributed to NaOH "eliminating non-cellulosic elements." Elimination/dissolution of non-cellulosic material from a fixed initial mass should decrease, not increase, the retained dry mass fraction. The paper provides no mass-balance evidence that higher yield instead reflects improved recovery, different starting moisture, or different processing losses. Thus the stated mechanistic explanation does not follow from the data.

Fibers of about 0.2 mm diameter and reported strength around 288 MPa would fail at roughly 9 N, not 5 kN. Yet the methods state that each 20-mm fiber was "subjected to a load of 5 kN." A 5-kN force on a ~0.03 mm² fiber would imply stress of order 10^5 MPa, physically incompatible with the reported tensile properties. The authors likely mean a 5-kN machine/load-cell capacity, but the stated testing load is incorrect and must be corrected.

predicted_errors.error_location: Density procedure immediately preceding Eq. (3), and Abstract
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The procedure calls the pycnometer result "absolute density" while immersing untreated lignocellulosic fibers in water for 24 h. These fibers are explicitly reported elsewhere to absorb 141-159% water. Water uptake during the displacement measurement invalidates a simple water-pycnometer calculation of dry absolute density unless absorption is prevented or a correction is made; no such correction is described. The resulting reported range, 0.633-1.522 g cm−3, is also inconsistent with an intrinsic/absolute density measurement: 0.633 g cm−3 is a bulk/apparent density, not a plausible pycnometric density for a cellulose/lignin solid. The paper conflates apparent/bulk density with absolute density.

The abstract concludes from FTIR that cellulose, hemicellulose, and lignin functional groups "are dissolved considerably as the percentage of NaOH increases." ATR-FTIR identifies bands at a surface and may show relative spectral changes, but it does not directly measure dissolution or quantify removal of cellulose, hemicellulose, or lignin without calibrated compositional analysis, mass balances, and appropriate spectral normalization. The stated dissolution conclusion is substantially stronger than the described measurement supports.

The water treatment involves two sequential 14-day retting stages followed by rinsing and 24 h of sun drying, whereas NaOH treatment is direct boiling for 2 h followed by neutralization and 72 h of sun drying. Yield is calculated only as dried recovered mass divided by initial mass, with no stated replicate extractions, no moisture correction for the initial pseudostem mass, and no uncertainty for the four yield values. Consequently, the reported differences cannot be attributed specifically to NaOH concentration or extraction chemistry; they are confounded by fundamentally different processing and recovery procedures.

The paper claims a MANOVA testing the influence of extraction method, but it describes only one collection site and does not state the number of independent pseudostems, independent extraction batches, or biological replicates per treatment. The listed 25 tensile fibers and five bundles/samples are subsamples from an unspecified extraction batch, not demonstrated independent experimental units. Treating such subsamples as independent treatment replicates would be pseudoreplication, so inferential claims about extraction method are not supported by the stated design.

predicted_errors.error_location: Figures 0-6 as supplied; references to Figs. 3-5 in Sections 2-3
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The embedded raster figures do not correspond to their captions or to the claimed papaya-fiber data. For example, the images labelled Figure 0 through Figure 5 consist of unrelated, densely typeset material rather than photographs of submerged pseudostems, extracted fibers, an extraction-yield plot, or a diameter plot. The text refers to Fig. 3a-d as extraction photographs, Fig. 4 as an extraction-yield curve, and Fig. 5 as a diameter curve, but no corresponding intelligible figures are supplied. This is a serious figure-content/caption mismatch requiring replacement with the actual figures.

predicted_errors.error_location: Section 3.1.1, first sentence and Table caption labelled Fig. 4
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The prose says "Fig. 3 shows that fiber yield (Fig. 4) and texture are influenced," while the displayed item captioned "Fig. 4. Extraction yield distribution curve" is a four-value table rather than a distribution curve. The figure numbering and descriptions are internally confused, preventing verification of the yield claim.

predicted_errors.error_location: Abstract, final conclusion that 2.5% NaOH is "the most suitable for biocomposite applications"
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The conclusion selects 2.5% NaOH as optimal based principally on single-fiber tensile results with very large variability (287.55 ± 56 MPa strength; 8.271 ± 1.62 modulus; 3.505 ± 1.01% elongation), while the paper itself states that diameter affected results and that there is a need to study technique and NaOH mass concentration. No composite fabrication, interfacial adhesion test, composite mechanical test, or demonstrated statistical comparison establishing superiority is reported. Therefore a conclusion about suitability for biocomposite applications is unsupported by the presented evidence.
